subject: margay cat
title: A Wild Cat Imitates Baby Monkey Cries to Lure the Parents In

scenes.text: This cat does a baby monkey impression. And it's a hunting trick.
The margay. Seven pounds of spotted cat in the Amazon treetops.
In 2005, scientists in Brazil watched eight tamarin monkeys feeding in a fig tree. Then a baby tamarin cried from the vines.
It wasn't a baby. It was the margay, copying the call. A lookout monkey climbed down to check. Four more followed.
The cat slipped out and walked down the trunk toward them. That time the lookout caught on, and they fled.
The first wild cat in the Americas ever recorded faking its prey's voice. Locals say jaguars do it too.

description:
A margay, a small spotted cat of the Amazon, was recorded imitating the cries of a baby pied tamarin to draw adult monkeys within reach.
Wildlife Conservation Society researchers saw it in 2005 in Brazil's Adolpho Ducke reserve: the fake call pulled a sentinel and four other tamarins down toward the cat before the group caught on and fled. Published in Neotropical Primates (2009), it is the first documented case of vocal mimicry by a wild cat in the Americas; local accounts say jaguars and pumas do it too.
What's the sneakiest hunting trick you know? Comment below.
first_comment: The researchers said the impression was a poor one, but good enough to confuse the monkeys. They think margay mothers teach the trick to their kittens. Which animal trickster should we cover next?
